title: Roman Omens and Prodigies
lead: Romans looked for the gods' mind in storms, birds, the entrails of sacrificed animals and strange births, and Tacitus records many such signs in AD 69. The Bible forbids divination (Deuteronomy 18:10-12) yet shows pagan rulers using it (Ezekiel 21:21).

sections.b: Wikipedia says a haruspex inspected the entrails of sacrificed animals, especially the liver, to judge whether the gods approved of an action, a craft Rome took from the Etruscans and that Babylonians practiced too. In Book 1 the haruspex Umbricius reads gloomy entrails for Galba (1:27); thunder and lightning mark the day of Piso's adoption (1:18); Tacitus lists a chariot's reins slipping, a form bursting from a shrine and a speaking ox (1:86). He also notes that astrologers are both forbidden and kept at Rome (1:22).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:18; Histories of Tacitus 1:22; Histories of Tacitus 1:27; Histories of Tacitus 1:86

sections.b: "The king of Babylon has halted where the road splits... He examines the liver" (Ezekiel 21:21). Isaiah mocks the Babylonian astrologers, "the ones who map out the sky" (Isaiah 47:13). Jesus says people can tell what the face of the sky means but cannot read "the signs of the times" (Matthew 16:3), and he speaks of "great signs from the sky" before the end (Luke 21:11).
